newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Tietmeyer -- EMU may fail without strict pact.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Tietmeyer -- EMU may fail without strict pact.

text.p: German Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer warned on Thursday that political conflicts could tear apart Europe's planned common currency if member states did not agree to a strict stability pact to defend it.
Tietmeyer said an unstable economic and monetary union (EMU) could unleash "centrifugal forces" creating more tension among member states rather than greater integration.

"We are in favour of a hard currency union and against a weak currency union. Fiscal discipline must be secured, or else the danger the EMU could be torn apart is very high," he told Bonn journalists. "Then we'd be worse off than we are today."

Bundesbank council member Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher echoed this in a speech in Berlin, saying an EMU collapse "would signal a step backwards in the process of European integration, leading to a return of individual economic policies."
Another Bundesbank council member, Ernst Welteke, said he feared Germany and France would miss meeting deficit criteria in 1997 for membership in the single European currency.
A spokesman for the regional state central bank of Hesse confirmed the statement that Welteke made in an interview with Market News Service.
Welteke also told the news service in an interview that the start of currency union for 1999 was still possible but that talk of a delay was unwise.
Tietmeyer rebutted charges he was against the Euro currency due in 1999, saying he was a "realistic European" convinced of the need for a stable and credible EMU right from the start.
That was why he backed the stability pact proposed by Finance Minister Theo Waigel, with penalties to ensure members' deficits kept within three percent of gross domestic product.

But he said EMU entry did not depend solely on meeting the deficit target and the debt limit of 60 percent of GDP because the Maastricht Treaty allowed for some interpretation of those criteria in the light of economic developments.
"The figures and the qualifying comments (in the treaty) must be strictly interpreted," he stressed.
The main problem with EMU, Tietmeyer said, was that member states will continue pursuing mostly national economic policies and have only their monetary policy in common.

"We will still have national financial policies and national social policies," he said. "Centrifugal forces could quickly arise here if there is not at least a common measure of fiscal discipline, and it must be permanent fiscal discipline."

If an EMU member did not keep pace with the others, he said, this could lead to higher interest rates within the whole currency region, higher unemployment in the region involved and calls for transfer payments from Brussels or the other states.
The stronger countries could end up turning on the poor performer or getting enmeshed in debates over what the European Central Bank should do about the problem, Tietmeyer said.
"Those are the potential conflicts -- and I could name even more cases -- if the convergence is not sufficient," he said.
The new currency zone to be created with the Euro currency could not be compared to large national economies like the United States, Tietmeyer added.
"In the nation-state, one has these automatic unifying forces like a common tax system, a common legal system, a central budget and a common social system," he said.
"In the nation-state, there is a comomon solidarity," he said. "We do not have this form of solidarity on the European level. We won't have that in Europe for a long time."
Tietmeyer shrugged off a bitter attack by former Chancellor Helmut Schmidt last week accusing him of playing the monetary strongman in Europe and creating resentment against Germany.
"I am an oak," he remarked with a smile.

Rejecting the suggestion that Germany was using its economic power to get its own way in Europe, he said smaller EU members had told him they backed the stability pact because it would also discipline the larger states like Germany.
"The stability pact is aimed at us as well," he said. "It's not just a message from the first in the class. If someone is to be the first in the class, well, the Dutch are ahead of the others."
